Area $A_{1}$ enclosed by curves

$\begin{array}{l} 8-x=x^{2}+2 \\ x^{2}+x-6=0 \\ x^{2}+3x-2x-6=0 \\ x(x+3)-2(x+3)=0 \\ (x+3)(x-2)=0 \\ x=-3,2 \end{array}$

solution.body:
$\cot x=\frac{5}{12},x\in \left (π,\frac{3π}{2}\right )$ means 3rd quadrant.

To find the value of:

$\sin 7x\left (\cos \frac{13x}{2}+\sin \frac{13x}{2}\right )+\cos 7x\left (\cos \frac{13x}{2}-\sin \frac{13x}{2}\right )$

Simplify:

$=\sin 7x\cos \frac{13x}{2}+\sin 7x\sin \frac{13x}{2}+\cos 7x\cos \frac{13x}{2}-\sin \frac{13x}{2}\cos 7x$

Rearranging terms and use $\sin A\cos B-\cos A\sin B=\sin (A-B)$ and $\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B=\cos (A-B)$ :

$\begin{array}{l} =\sin 7x\cos \dfrac{13x}{2}-\sin \dfrac{13x}{2}\cos 7x+\cos 7x\cos \dfrac{13x}{2}+\sin 7x\sin \dfrac{13x}{2} \\ =\sin \left (7x-\dfrac{13x}{2}\right )+\cos \left (7x-\dfrac{13x}{2}\right ) \\ =\sin \dfrac{x}{2}+\cos \dfrac{x}{2} \end{array}$

Since $x\in \left (π,\frac{3π}{2}\right )$, then $\frac{x}{2}\in \left (\frac{π}{2},\frac{3π}{4}\right )$.

Let $L=\sin \frac{x}{2}+\cos \frac{x}{2}$.

In the second quadrant, $\frac{x}{2}$ makes $L$ positive because $\sin \frac{x}{2}>\left |\cos \frac{x}{2}\right |$.

Squaring:

$L^{2}=\sin ^{2}\frac{x}{2}+\cos ^{2}\frac{x}{2}+2\sin \frac{x}{2}\cos \frac{x}{2}$

$L^{2}=1+\sin x=1+\frac{1}{\mathrm{cosec}x}=1+\frac{1}{-\sqrt{1+\cot ^{2}x}}$, Since $x$ is in the 3rd quadrant, $\sin x$ must be negative

$L^{2}=1+\frac{1}{-\sqrt{1+\frac{25}{144}}}\left (\text{Since}\cot x=\frac{5}{12}\right )$

$L^{2}=1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{169}{144}}}=1-\frac{12}{13}=\frac{1}{13}$

$L=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}$

Let $\log _{e}t=x$.

$\begin{array}{l} t=e^{x}\Rightarrow dt=e^{x}dx \\ f(t)=\int \left (\dfrac{1-\sin x}{1-\cos x}\right )e^{x}dx \\ =\int \left (\dfrac{1-2\sin \frac{x}{2}\cos \frac{x}{2}}{2\sin ^{2}\frac{x}{2}}\right )e^{x}dx\left \{\begin{array}{l} \text{use}\sin 2θ=2\sin θ\cos θ \\ 1-\cos 2θ=2\sin ^{2}θ \end{array}\right \} \\ f(t)=\int \left [\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}-\cot \dfrac{x}{2}\right ]e^{x}dx \end{array}$

This standard integral of type $\int e^{x}[g(x)+g^{'}(x)]=e^{x}\cdot g(x)+C$.

$\begin{array}{l} -e^{π/2}=-e^{π/2}\cot \left (\dfrac{\log _{e}e^{π/2}}{2}\right )+C \\ -e^{π/2}=-e^{π/2}\cot \left (\dfrac{π}{4}\right )+C \\ -e^{π/2}=-e^{π/2}+C\Rightarrow C=0 \end{array}$

using result $1+\cos 2θ=2\cos ^{2}θ...(1)$

$\begin{array}{l} \sin 2θ=2\sin θ\cos θ \\ \dfrac{1+\cos 2θ}{\sin 2θ}=\dfrac{2\cos ^{2}θ}{2\sin θ\cos θ}=\cot θ...(2) \end{array}$

$α=-\cot \left (\frac{π}{8}\right )=-\left (\frac{1+\cos \frac{π}{4}}{\sin \frac{π}{4}}\right )$

$α=-\left (\frac{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\right )=-(\sqrt{2}+1)$.

solution.body:
$729,81,9,1,\ldots$ is a sequence in G.P. Can be written as $9^{3},9^{2},9^{1},9^{0},\frac{1}{9},\left (\frac{1}{9}\right )^{2},\ldots$

$P_{n}$ is the product of the first $n$ terms

$\begin{array}{l} P_{n}=\left (9^{3}\right )\left (9^{2}\right )\left (9^{1}\right )\ldots  \\ P_{n}=9^{3+2+1+0+(-1)+(-2)\ldots } \end{array}$

Clearly powers of 9 are in A.P. with first term $=3$

common difference $=-1$

So, sum of first $n$ terms of this A.P. $=\frac{n}{2}[2\times 3+(n-1)(-1)]$

$=\frac{n}{2}[6-n+1]=\frac{n}{2}(7-n)$

So, $P_{n}=(9)^{\frac{n}{2}(7-n)}$

It is given that

$\begin{array}{l} 2\sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}(P_{n})^{1/n}=\dfrac{3^{α}-1}{3^{β}} \\ \text{Solving} \\ \begin{array}{l} \sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}(P_{n})^{1/n}=\sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}(9)^{\frac{n}{2}(7-n)\times \frac{1}{n}}=\sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}9^{\frac{7-n}{2}} \\ \sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}\left (9^{1/2}\right )^{7-n}=\sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}(3)^{7-n}=3^{7}\sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}\left (\dfrac{1}{3}\right )^{n} \\ =3^{7}\left [\dfrac{1}{3}+\left (\dfrac{1}{3}\right )^{2}+\left (\dfrac{1}{3}\right )^{3}\cdots \left (\dfrac{1}{3}\right )^{40}\right ] \\ =3^{7}\left [\text{G.P. with first term}=\dfrac{1}{3}\text{common ratio}=\dfrac{1}{3}\right ] \end{array} \\ =3^{7}\times \dfrac{1}{3}\left [\dfrac{1-\left (\frac{1}{3}\right )^{40}}{1-\frac{1}{3}}\right ] \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}(P_{n})^{1/n}=3^{6}\left (\dfrac{\frac{3^{40}-1}{3^{40}}}{\frac{2}{3}}\right )=\dfrac{3^{40}-1}{2\cdot 3^{33}} \\ 2\sum\limits _{n=1}^{40}(P_{n})^{1/n}=\dfrac{3^{40}-1}{3^{33}}=\dfrac{3^{α}-1}{3^{β}} \\ \text{Comparing}α=40,β=33 \\ \text{g.c.d}(40,33)=1 \\ \text{So}α+β=40+33=73 \end{array}$

text: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy the equation $\int\limits _{0}^{36}f\left (\frac{tx}{36}\right )dt=4αf(x)$. If $y=f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through the points $(2,1)$ and $(-4,β)$, then $β^{α}$ is equal to $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given, $\int\limits _{0}^{36}f\left (\frac{tx}{36}\right )dt=4αf(x)$

Let $\frac{tx}{36}=u\Rightarrow \frac{x}{36}dt=du$

$\int\limits _{0}^{x}f(u)\frac{36}{x}du=4αf(x)$

Integration is w.r.t $u$, so treat $x$ as a constant

$\int\limits _{0}^{x}f(u)du=\frac{4x}{36}αf(x)=\frac{x}{9}αf(x)$

Now, differentiate both sides w.r.t $x$, use Leibniz theorem in LHS:

$1\cdot f(x)=\frac{α}{9}[1\cdot f(x)+xf^{'}(x)]$

$\Rightarrow$ $9f(x)=αf(x)+αxf^{'}(x)$

$\Rightarrow$ $αxf^{'}(x)=f(x)(9-α)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{9-α}{αx}$

Integrating both sides

$\int \frac{f^{'}(x)}{f(x)}dx=\int \frac{9-α}{α}\left (\frac{1}{x}\right )dx$

$\Rightarrow$ $\ln f(x)=\frac{9-α}{α}\ln x+c$

$\Rightarrow$ $f(x)=e^{\frac{9-α}{α}\ln x}\cdot e^{c}$

$\Rightarrow$ $f(x)=x^{\frac{9-α}{α}}\cdot K\{K=e^{c}\}$

It is given that $f(x)$ is a standard parabola passing through $(2,1)$ and $(-4,β)$.

So $f(x)=Kx^{2}$ type.

$\frac{9-α}{α}=2⟹9-α=2α⟹3α=9$

$\Rightarrow$ $α=3$

$f(x)=Kx^{2}$ passing through $(2,1)$

$f(2)=1$

$1=K(2)^{2}⟹K=\frac{1}{4}$

$f(x)=\frac{1}{4}x^{2}$

$f(x)$ is also passing through $(-4,β),f(-4)=β$

$β=\frac{1}{4}(-4)^{2}=\frac{16}{4}=4$

then $β^{α}=4^{3}=64$

text: The number of numbers greater than 5000 , less than 9000 and divisible by 3 , that can be formed using the digits $0,1,2,5,9$, if the repetition of the digits is allowed, is $____$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 24th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A number between 5000 and 9000 formed from the digits $0,1,2,5,9$ has 4 digits with thousands digit 5 (a thousands digit 9 gives a number of at least 9000), so $N=5abc–$ with $a,b,c\in \{0,1,2,5,9\}$.

$N$ is divisible by 3 when $5+a+b+c$ is a multiple of 3, that is, when $a+b+c\equiv 1(\mathrm{mod}3)$.

Remainders of the digits on division by 3: $0,9\to 0$ (2 digits), $1\to 1$ (1 digit), $2,5\to 2$ (2 digits). For each choice of $(a,b)$, the remainder of $c$ is then fixed.

$a+b\equiv 0$: remainder pairs $(0,0)$ give $2\times 2=4$ and $(1,2),(2,1)$ give $2+2=4$, so 8 pairs; $c\equiv 1$ allows only $c=1$, giving $8\times 1=8$ numbers.

$a+b\equiv 1$: remainder pairs $(0,1),(1,0)$ give $2+2=4$ and $(2,2)$ gives $2\times 2=4$, so 8 pairs; $c\equiv 0$ allows $c\in \{0,9\}$, giving $8\times 2=16$ numbers.

$a+b\equiv 2$: remainder pairs $(0,2),(2,0)$ give $4+4=8$ and $(1,1)$ gives 1, so 9 pairs; $c\equiv 2$ allows $c\in \{2,5\}$, giving $9\times 2=18$ numbers.

Total $=8+16+18=42$.

Hence, the answer is 42.
